planting.note: Plant grafted or seedling container-grown trees in spring in deep, moist, well-drained soil in full sun; this West African rainforest tree is frost tender and suited only to zone 10-12 in the continental US, such as extreme South Florida or Hawaii.

directions: African star apple is a large, fast-growing rainforest tree of West and Central Africa distinct from the more familiar Caribbean star apple (Chrysophyllum cainito), bearing egg-shaped orange to yellow fruit with sweet, gelatinous, milky pulp around several flattened seeds arranged in a star pattern. Plant in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, since seedlings do not tolerate heavy shade; young trees need consistent moisture but established specimens handle brief dry spells once their root system is developed. Trees are naturally very large in the wild but can be kept to a manageable orchard size with regular structural pruning, and seedling trees are slow to bear, often taking many years, so grafted stock is preferable where available. Fruit is harvested when it softens slightly and turns fully orange or yellow, then eaten fresh by squeezing the pulp free of the tough skin, avoiding the sticky white latex in the unripe rind.

planting.note: Plant divisions or nursery-grown offshoots in spring in humus-rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade; Pondoh is a selection from Sleman, Yogyakarta prized for fruit that can be eaten immediately without the astringency of seedling salak.

directions: Salak Pondoh is Indonesia's most widely planted salak selection, originating from the Sleman district of Yogyakarta, valued for dry, crumbly-textured flesh that is sweet and only mildly acidic even before full ripeness, unlike the sharp, astringent bite of unimproved seedling salak. Grow this clumping, spiny-trunked palm in rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in the dappled shade of taller trees, since salak is naturally an understory plant of humid tropical forests. Female plants need a male pollinator nearby, or hand pollination, to ensure good fruit set, and mature clumps should have excess suckers and spent leaves removed regularly to keep the planting productive and manageable. Harvest fruit clusters when the overlapping reddish-brown scales lift slightly and the fruit gives a bit to gentle pressure.

planting.note: Plant divisions or nursery-grown offshoots in spring in humus-rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade; Salak Bali is the classic snake fruit of Bali, larger-fruited than Pondoh with moist, crunchy rather than dry, crumbly flesh.

directions: Salak Bali is the traditional snake fruit of Bali, grown for centuries around villages in the island's eastern regency of Karangasem, and is distinguished from the Java-bred Pondoh type by its larger fruit and moist, crunchy, juicier flesh with a sweet-tart flavor rather than Pondoh's dry, crumbly texture. Like other salak, it is a low, clumping, viciously spined palm best grown in the filtered light of an open woodland canopy in rich, constantly moist, well-drained soil; full tropical heat and humidity are essential, and the palm will not tolerate any frost. Because salak is dioecious, keep a male plant or take cuttings of male inflorescences nearby for hand pollination to guarantee heavy fruit set on female clumps. Manage clumps by removing excess suckers and old fronds, and harvest fruit in tight clusters once the snakeskin-like scales are fully colored and the fruit yields slightly to pressure.

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring in rich, moist, well-drained soil in full sun sheltered from strong wind; Rongrien is Thailand's leading commercial rambutan cultivar and the selection most often recommended for South Florida because of its dependable bearing and consistent flavor.

directions: Rongrien is the most widely planted rambutan cultivar in Thailand and the variety most commonly recommended for South Florida growers, prized for its hermaphroditic flowering, which allows reliable self-pollination and fruit set without a separate pollinator tree. Grafted Rongrien trees come into bearing markedly faster than seedling rambutan and produce clusters of bright red, soft-spined fruit with sweet, easily separated flesh. Grow in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun protected from strong wind, keeping soil evenly moist through flowering and fruit development since drought stress during these stages sharply reduces yield. Like all rambutan, it has essentially no cold tolerance and needs consistently warm, humid, frost-free conditions, making it suitable only for the warmest parts of zone 10b and above.

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring in rich, moist, well-drained soil in full sun sheltered from strong wind; Binjai is a heavy-yielding Indonesian rambutan cultivar with attractive red, spherical fruit and comparatively firm, less juicy flesh.

directions: Binjai is a popular Indonesian rambutan cultivar renowned for exceptionally heavy yields and attractive, spherical, red-skinned fruit covered in soft red spines. The aril is comparatively firm and less juicy than other cultivars, with high sugar content that makes it a favorite for fresh eating, and fruit holds its quality for a few days after harvest better than many softer-fleshed rambutan selections. Grow grafted trees in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun with wind protection, providing steady moisture through bloom and fruit set to maximize the cultivar's naturally high productivity. As with all rambutan, Binjai has no frost tolerance and requires warm, humid, essentially tropical conditions year-round, restricting it to the warmest microclimates of zone 10b and above.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Red Tip is the upright, larger-growing inland form of cocoplum, distinguished by bright red-bronze new growth that matures to glossy dark green.

directions: Red Tip Cocoplum is the upright inland form of the native Florida cocoplum, grown as much for its ornamental flush of bright red to orange-bronze new leaves as for its small, dark purple, plum-like edible fruit used in jellies and preserves. Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; it grows larger and less salt-tolerant than the low, spreading 'Horizontal' coastal form, making it better suited to hammock-style gardens and hedges than beachfront plantings. Established plants tolerate heat, humidity, and periodic flooding well, and respond to shearing with dense, twiggy regrowth, making it a popular clipped hedge or screen throughout South Florida landscapes. Clusters of small white flowers appear through summer, followed by fruit that ripens over an extended season and should be picked as it colors fully for the best flavor.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in sandy, well-drained soil in full sun; Horizontal is the low, spreading coastal ecotype of cocoplum, valued for its salt tolerance and use as a groundcover on beach-edge plantings.

directions: Horizontal Cocoplum is the naturally low, creeping coastal form of Florida's native cocoplum, selected for its dense, spreading habit and outstanding salt and wind tolerance compared to the taller, upright 'Red Tip' inland form. Its trailing branches root readily where they touch the ground, gradually knitting together into a dense mat that is excellent for stabilizing dunes, beach edges, and other exposed coastal sites prone to erosion. Plant in full sun in sandy, well-drained soil; once established it needs little supplemental irrigation and tolerates salt spray, wind, and poor soil far better than most fruiting shrubs. It still produces the species' small, edible, dark purple fruit, though its primary garden role is as a tough, low-maintenance groundcover for coastal landscapes.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or grafted plants in spring after frost danger passes; Sertaneja (registered as BRS 152) is a Brazilian EMBRAPA-bred acerola cultivar selected for productivity and fruit quality under the hot, semi-arid conditions of Brazil's Northeast.

directions: Sertaneja, registered as BRS 152, is one of a series of acerola cultivars released by Brazil's EMBRAPA agricultural research agency, bred for reliable production and good fruit quality in the hot, drought-prone growing regions of Brazil, the world's leading acerola-producing country. Grow in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil, watering regularly during establishment and through flowering and fruit set, though the cultivar tolerates brief dry spells better than many other tropical fruiting shrubs once established. Like other acerola selections it flowers and fruits in repeated flushes through the warm season, yielding small, bright red, extremely vitamin C-rich fruit that must be harvested and used within a day or two of ripening. Light pruning after each fruiting flush keeps the shrub compact and encourages continued flowering.

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; the yellow type of santol is distinguished by leaves that turn yellow rather than red before falling, and by its thinner-rinded, sweeter fruit.

directions: Yellow santol is the sweeter of the two long-recognized forms of santol, formerly classified as a separate species (Sandoricum indicum) before both were merged into Sandoricum koetjape as varieties distinguished mainly by leaf color in fall and fruit character. Its thinner-skinned fruit has a comparatively thick, mild, sweet layer of cottony pulp around the seeds, making it the preferred type for fresh eating rather than processing. Grow in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun with steady moisture, giving the large canopy plenty of room to develop; grafted trees fruit within a few years while seedlings take considerably longer. Harvest when the smooth skin turns fully yellow and use fresh, or in preserves and candies as with the more common red type.

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; the red type of santol, the form most commonly sold commercially, has leaves that turn red before falling and a thicker rind than the yellow type.

directions: Red santol is the form most widely grown and sold commercially throughout Southeast Asia, historically distinguished as its own species (Sandoricum nervosum) before taxonomists merged it with the yellow type into a single species, Sandoricum koetjape, differentiated chiefly by its old leaves turning red rather than yellow before dropping and by a thicker rind around a thinner, more tart layer of pulp. Plant in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, allowing ample room for the tree's eventual large canopy, and provide consistent moisture through the growing season for best fruit set. Grafted selections come into bearing within a few years, whereas seedling trees take considerably longer. Harvest the round, downy, yellow-brown fruit once fully colored and slightly soft, and use the tangy, cottony pulp fresh or cooked into preserves and candied treats, as is traditional in the Philippines and Thailand.

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade; tampoi is a Bornean rainforest understory tree that fruits within two to three years and needs consistently warm, humid, frost-free conditions.

directions: Tampoi is a small to medium Bornean rainforest tree grown for its golden-yellow, spherical fruit borne in small clusters directly on the trunk and branches, each containing soft, juicy, off-white flesh ranging from sweet to pleasantly sour. As an understory species of humid lowland forest, it grows best in the dappled or partial shade of taller trees rather than in open, exposed sun, and needs rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil to thrive. Trees begin fruiting within two to three years of planting and require relatively little maintenance beyond regular watering during dry spells and periodic light fertilizing. Harvest fruit clusters once the skin turns fully golden-yellow and gives slightly to pressure, and eat the fresh pulp out of hand, since tampoi does not ship or store well.
